description.narrative:
Saferworld is an independent international organization that works with research, policy development, capacity building and implementation of programs aimed at preventing violence and conflict. Saferworld conducts conflict prevention and peacebuilding work in Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Europe. Currently, Saferworld's geographical focus is on the following countries: Kenya, Somalia / Somaliland, Sudan and South Sudan, Uganda, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal, Syria and Yemen.
By utilizing local knowledge and building on the experiences of conflict-affected individuals and society, Saferworld works to improve and strengthen local, national and international peacebuilding for long-term sustainable development.
Sida has received an application for core support from Saferworld. The proposal is to support Saferworld's new five-year strategic plan (2021-2025) with a total amount of SEK 90 800 000 over three years (1 April 2021 - 31 March 2024), which corresponds to approximately 13% percent of Saferworld's total budget. Part of the support will be earmarked with an average of SEK 5 million per year for the purpose of working with control and against the spread of small and light weapons, as well as compliance with the Arms Trade Treaty. Sida has contributed core support to Saferworld since 2014 and this will thus be a continuation of this collaboration

Saferworld är en oberoende internationell organisation som arbetar med forskning, policyutveckling, kapacitetsbyggande och genomförande av program med syfte att förhindra våld och konflikt. Saferworld bedriver konfliktförebyggande och fredsbyggande arbete i Afrika, Mellanöstern, Asien och Europa. För närvarande är Saferworlds geografiska fokus följande länder: Kenya, Somalia/ Somaliland, Sudan och Sydsudan, Uganda, Kirgizistan, Tadjikistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal, Syrien och Yemen.
Genom att tillvarata lokal kunskap och utgå från konfliktdrabbade individers och samhällets erfarenheter arbetar Saferworld för att förbättra och stärka lokalt, nationellt och internationellt fredsbyggande för långsiktig hållbar utveckling.
Sida har mottagit en ansökan om kärnstöd från Saferworld. Förslaget är att stödja Saferworlds nya femåriga strategiska plan (2021- 2025) med ett totalt belopp om 90 800 000 SEK över tre år (1 april 2021 - 31 mars 2024), vilket motsvarar cirka 13% procent av Saferworlds totala budget. En del av stödet kommer att öronmärkas med i genomsnitt 5 MSEK per år för ändamålet att arbeta med kontroll och mot spridning av små och lätta vapen, samt efterlevnad av Vapenhandelsfördraget. Sida har bidragit med kärnstöd till Saferworld sedan 2014 och detta blir därmed en fortsättning på detta samarbete.

To contribute to prevention of violent conflict and strengthen human security, the core support from Sida will, for the period 2021-2023, contribute to the following five interlinked goals set out in Saferworld's Strategic Plan Working in solidarity for a safer world 2021-2031: i) Inclusive peace and justice: Communities and CSOs, in particular women and youth, in conflict-affected contexts lead efforts to achieve conflict transformation and political transitions rooted in equality and justice by working with authorities and each other across conflict divides, and with relevant external actors. ii) People-centred security: External actors, governments, and state and non-state security actors increasingly recognise and move away from harmful militarised and repressive approaches to conflict and security, and towards a people-centred and more accountable understanding of human security. iii) Gender Equality: Donors, peacebuilding organisations and policymakers, communities, civil society and authorities address gender norms and patriarchal systems and structures driving exclusion, conflict and insecurity, and promote gender equality and womens meaningful participation and leadership through their programming and policies. iv) Redesigning international engagement: International actors in conflict-affected and fragile settings realign their systems, instruments and resources to underpin peaceful change and transformation from within, putting local leadership in the driving seat. v) Climate, conflict and the environment: Communities, CSOs, authorities (local, state, national) and international actors recognise the effects of climate change on conflict dynamics; collaboration between peacebuilding and environmental practitioners is strengthened; and strategies to incorporate climate change and conflict prevention are developed around more holistic responses

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
Under the Strategic Objective 1 (Inclusive peace and Justice), SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- Saferworld continued to work with communities to strengthen capacities to identify and address peace building and justice priorities in Kyrgyzstan, Myanmar, Sudan, Yemen and Somalia/Somaliland, Kenya and Uganda. For example; strengthening mental health and psychological support self- support groups in Kyrgyzstan, continued work with community legal volunteers (CLVs), who serve as part of the community- based access to justice mechanism in Myanmar, peace building activities in Somalia/Somaliland (addressing tensions over access to water and pasture) including support to national reconciliation efforts led by the Somaliland government through the Yaqoori Peace process.For example, in Kenya, SW together with local partners, supported the cross- border West Pokot Marakwet Peace Committee (through peace dialogues) to defuse tensions in the area caused by conflicts which had involved cattle raids and killings. In addition, SW also conducted peace interventions in Kasei and Sarmach wards to mitigate the conflict situation along the Kainuk Turkwel Corridor. This process was initiated at the request of local partners and brought together herders, women and Kraal elders to discuss the issues that exacerbate conflicts, namely underdevelopment, political incitement, cross- border tensions over resources, and prolonged drought. As a result, communities became more willing to enter into dialogues with herders from neighbouring wards in Turkana South. In Uganda, SW together with local partners have supported Community Action Groups (CAGs), a dispute resolution and cognitive behavioural therapy groups, through training and linking them to advocacy efforts at sub- national and national levels through policy briefs and discussions. As a result of their increased confidence, capacity and leadership in their communities, a considerable number of CAG members have gone on to work in their communities as community social workers, and som have been elected as councillors, chairpersons and members of area land committees across the project's target districts. In Sudan, SF supported community- led initiatives to address the wide spectrum of conflict resolution, peace building, justice and humanitarian issues and priorities that were generated or which increased massively due to the conflict raging across the country. Community dialogue sessions were facilitated that brought together communities and groups in conflict - such as host communities, IDPS, returnees and local administrations - to foster mutual understanding and collaboration. A significant aspect of these initiatives was the formation of local and cross-line peace committees.
- In Sudan, 750 community initiatives were supported through micro- grants. These initiatives were implemented in ten out of 18 states and focused on strengthening the co-existence and cohesion, supporting spaces for dialogue among youth and civil society actors to reduce fragmentation and develop a common vision for peace, and responding to the humanitarian crises. SW also continued with flexible support to CSOs and coalitions in Myanmar, Somalia, Sudan, Yemen and Kenya. The Yemen Civil Society Fund which was launched in 2019 continued to provide grants of up to 45 000 USD to Yemeni CSOs to enhance their roles as peacebuilders. So far, the fund has supported 18 organizations, for example, the Basmat Hayat for People with Disabilities, which has used the grants to improve their financial and administrative performance to be able to continue their work on the integration of people with disabilities into the Yemeni society. In Taiz, another community based organisations was supported under the fund to address the urgent needs of young people in juvenile detention.
Under Strategic Objective 2 (people- centered security), SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- In Sudan, amid ongoing war and the breakdown of many formal public institutions, traditional leaders in South Nyala stepped in to address the rise in criminality and unresolved community grievances. Trained in legal procedures and equipped with necessary resources, the traditional leaders reinstated local order, demonstrating the effectiveness of traditional justice mechanisms in maintaining and resolving dispute during crisis.
- In Somalia, a civilian oversight model was designed to involve civilians directly in overseeing security operations, raising public concerns and ensuring these are addressed. The process involved engaging security ministers, creating ad hoc committees with public and government representatives, and holding public dialogues to disseminate information and gather feedback. The formulation of this model reflects a commitment to participatory governance whereby diverse community voices shape security policies and oversight mechanisms. In Kismayo, the Director General of the Jubaland Ministry of Justice has shown increase leadership and commitment to public dialogues by actively participating in and co- facilitating participatory public policy dialogues - this highlights senior officials' stronger engagement with, and ownership of, community- focused initiatives. Furthermore, participants from marginalized groups, including IDPs, people with disabilities, women's rights organisations and minorities, expressed greater confidence by directly raising concerns with senior security and justice representatives during these dialogues.
- In Kenya, border peace committees, supported by SW and their local partners, collaborated with national government structures (at the community level) to recover stolen livestock. Ongoing collaboration between the board peace committees and national government structures will improve the security services' response to incidents and improve communities' real and perceived security.
- In Kyrgyzstan, crime prevention action plans for 11 local crime prevention centres (LCPDCs) were supported. These action plans are aimed at addressing a range of critical community issues, particularly those concerning young people, for example drug abuse. LPCs also contribute to the prevention of GBV through awareness initiatives. 11 outreach campaigns were conducted by juvenile police inspectors across seven provinces.
- In Yemen, two CSO hubs (in Taiz and Aden) were supported through small grants to improve public services. The hubs are working in challenging circumstances to enhance community security and peace through a variety of activities: strengthening the capacity of judicial and administrative staff, prosecution offices and Taiz Police Department staff; establishing complaints and reports mechanism; deploying surveillance cameras; integrating returnees and juvenile detainees into society; and advocating to authorities for issues that affect people's daily lives, including water, sanitation, electricity and security.
- In South Sudan, state governments in Lakes and Warrap States were engaged on the insecurity at the joint border between Cueibet County and Tonj South County which resulted in interventions by both the Acting County Commissioner and the Panyjar County Commissioner. As a result, cattle raiding was reduced between Mayendit and Koch counties in Unity State and cattle were returned to the neighboring community in Rumbek East County. This is significant not only for the immediate improvement in security but also because of an increase in trust and peaceful co-existence.
Under Strategic Objective 3 (Gender- equality), SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- In South Sudan, stakeholders from Central Equatoria, Eastern Equatoria and Jonglei States discussed, in conference organized by SW and their partners, how gender stereotypes and norms are barriers for peace building efforts and conflict prevention. Following this, the State Ministries of Gender, Child and Social Welfare across all three states signed resolutions to demonstrate their commitment to ending early and forced marriages.
- In Somalia, 150 women activists from Jubaland and South West participated in a women's forum that strengthened connections and established a learning network across the country, and 300 women volunteers who received training continue to safely monitor and track incidents and patterns of GBV against women activists in these states. Through technical skills training to 50 activists from 20 women- led organisations, there has been an increased in the number of women activists and journalists reporting on GBV and referring others to available GBV services and protection mechanisms.
- Under Saferworld' flagship programme "Resourcing Change: Supporting women's rights organisations in fragile and conflict- affected states", the independent role of WROs in leading programming and advocacy in peace building, gender equality, women's empowerment and participation, and GBV prevention and response continued to be strengthened. Through core, flexible and easily accessible funds to support capacity strengthening and increased movement- building, 23 WROs and two women's hubs were able to deliver on WPS agendas in Nigeria, South Sudan and Yemen. As a result of the project's positive outcomes, additonal funding of 50 000 British pound was secured in the October 2023 to support women's participation at WPS week in New York, a global forum for those working on WPS. The Resourcing Change consortium co- convened a side event with the UK mission and UN Women, where a report was launched on localising the WPS agenda.
- In South Sudan, in Eastern Equatoria state, SW together with local partners advocated for the inclusion of women in customary court settings and for the county commissioner to respond to local-level insecurity caused by armed robbers. Together with local leaders, SF and their local partners, successfully lobbied the leaders in Awul Payam, Tonj North, to include five women as members of the customary court - the first time that women had participated in traditional justice mechanisms in Warrap State. As a result of women sitting in customary courts - until that point dominated by men - women police officers and court officials take charge of investigating cases of domestic violence, gender- based violence, and other women- related justice issues. Two women have also been appointed as chiefs and members of the customary court panel in Gakyuom Village, in BorSouth County, Jonglei State, overcoming the longstanding Dinka customary law that prohibited women from holding leadership positions. This marked a significant cultural shift and an accountability benchmark to UNSCR 1325 which emphasises the role of women in peace and security efforts. Women's representation in leadership structures has not only encouraged other women to pursue leadership roles in communities and within the customary court, but has also encouraged reporting of GBV cases.
Under Strategic Objective 4 (Redesigning international engagement), SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- SW completed their advisory work for the ADB and KfW - building on previous experience with the European Investment Bank (EIB). The team trained senior ADB staff on leadership in fragile, conflict- affected and small island developing states. The MTR of the ADB's strategy of fragile and conflict- affected situations and small island developing states contains promising recommendations on engaging civil society and integrating conflict sensitivity, particularly for programming in Afghanistan and Myanmar.
- SW worked with the humanitarian community in South Sudan, helping to create a conflict- sensitive decision- making matrix to guide tough choices on aid prioritization in the context of significant budget cuts. This ensured that conflict sensitivity was at the heart of strategic decisions coordinated by OCHA and taken by the humanitarian country team.
- SW and their partners succeeded in influencing the UN Security Council to alter the text of a resolution on human fraternity, preventing the inclusion of overly broad clauses on "extremism" and of regressive language on civic space and gender equality. A similar success came when the US, EU and Swiss organisations used SW's policy advice to protect human rights and civic space language in the eighth review of the UN Global Counter- Terrorism Strategy.
- When the process for producing the UN Secretary-General's policy brief on the New Agenda for Peace did not offer serious openings for civil society input, SW, together with partners, created a submission paper to the UN Secretariat team drafting the Agenda. The major focus issues of this paper - civic pace, securitisation, localisation and climate - all featured in the final New Agenda.
- In terms of supporting vertical and horizontal linkages and influencing authorities, SW also supported numerous initatives to strengthen the capacities of local partners. For example, SW actively facilitated the participation of Sudanese civil society partners in various international platforms to amplify their voices and perspectives on conflict transformation and advocate for peace in Sudan. This included engaging with members of the US Congress and officials from the Department of State and more.
Under Strategic Objective 5 (Climate, conflict and the environment), SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- SW has been actively participating in and contributing to global community of practice on environment, climate, conflict and peace, including as signatory to Peace@COP28 messaging on the importance of focusing on conflict and peace at COP28, highlighting conflict sensitivity issues in climate adaptation to influence policymakers at COP28. This included advocating for applying a peace and conflict lens to climate action, which resulted in much more prominent conflict sensitivity messaging in the related Declaration on Peace, Relief and Recovery this year.
- During the report period, SW has commissioned and published research into the links between climate change, conflict and conflict- sensitive aid, focusing on community perceptions and understanding based on field research across two different contexts in South Sudan. The research provided some valuable findings to improve aid actors' understanding of their engagement at this intersection.
- Funding was secured for three new programmes, focusing on working with partners across borderlands areas in East Africa (on conflict prevention, resilience and livelihoods, and on gender, climate, environmental issues and peace building) and in the Ferghana Valley in Central Asia through which civil society will be supported to build understanding and capacity on climatic issues and resource management, as well as linking up relevant actors across the region to work across borders on environmental issues.
Under the earmarked funding to sthrengthening SW's work on arms control, SaferWorld has reported many achievements under the reporting period, some of which are highlighted below:
- In April 2023, Saferworld, alongside its partners, launched the Arms Trade Litigation Monitor (ATLM), an independent interactive website which tracks and documents litigation and legal interventions relating to authorised arms exports. By the end of 2023, the ATLM was tracking around 27 cases across 11 jurisdictions (seven in Europe and four in other jurisdictions in North America, South Africa and the International Criminal Court, with more being added regularly). The ATLM has received significant engagement, with at least 1 000 users and approximately 36000 views recorded up to March 2024. ATLM has been cited as an important and useful resource in high- attendance external meetings, including a Forum on the Arms Trade event. Officials from multiple jurisdictions are following legal developments closely and SF has had official telling them that ATLM helped them keep up to date. The site also received significant positive feedback from several civil society partners for its potential to inspire and support legal challenges as well potentially exert significant pressure on governments regarding issues of collective action - and from academics, who have heralded it as an excellent resource for them and for the students.
- The small grants programme, that was launched in 2022, to support civil society in conflict- affected contexts to undertake projects related to tackling the proliferation and misuse of small arms and lights weapons, continued to support formal and informal civil society coalitions/groups, primarily based in the global south. For example, a project in Kenya engaged communities on SALW issues and raised awareness of the dangers of firearms- related violence. The project includes community awareness- raising forums at the county and sub- county levels, intergenerational dialogues to understand the drivers of violence and foster consensus on improving disarmament initiatives, and "peace days" to engage young people, women and elders on these issues through sports and theatre. The project also included weekly radio talk shows to discuss community concerns about SALW and allow individuals to share their experiences.
- In South Sudan, circular community- led discussions in local neighbourhoods, with 90 participants (39 women and 51 men) were held. These awareness raising dialogues highlighted a range of threats posed by SALW and their impact on civilian experiences of peace and security. The dialogues culminated in the participants calling for improved community- based solutions to SALW proliferation and misuse and initiatives to brings chiefs, young cattle herders and government representatives together to identify and address the threats posed by firearms.
- In Uganda, SW continued to examine the quantitative and qualitative data obtained through monitoring, evaluation and learning to understand the impacts of its small arms project. SW has facilitated outcome harvesting workshops to organisations working in this area for continuous learning and adaptation. SW has also developed mechanisms to share leanings and experience between the partners, which is particularly important given the geographical nature of the focus communities for the Uganda, South Sudan and Kenya projects, where a key driver of conflict is the illicit trade and proliferation of SALW across the countries' borders.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
